strengths: First large-scale, systematic empirical picture of who reports social impact evaluations for foundation models, covering 186 first-party release reports and 248 post-release sources across seven dimensions; this fills a genuine gap between normative documentation frameworks (model cards, FMTI) and actual practice.

Methodologically careful annotation effort: a well-motivated 0-3 ordinal scoring rubric with modified criteria for cost categories, substantial double-annotation (390 items, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.75/0.83), disagreement adjudication, and a rigorous Bayesian hierarchical ordinal regression analysis with sensitivity models including annotator-level random effects, LOO-CV model comparison, and full convergence diagnostics (App. L).

The mixed-method design is a real strength: the stakeholder interviews (10 semi-structured, with interview guide in App. N) contextualize the quantitative findings and yield the paper's most insightful claims, e.g., that evaluations run only when they 'support product adoption, directly affect business metrics, or if regulation forces us', and that environmental/bias reporting declines reflect shifting incentives rather than infeasibility.

Excellent transparency practices: explicit conflict-of-interest disclosure, an honest and substantive limitations section (small non-representative interview sample, regional bias, presence-not-quality focus), and a promised dataset release of model-level and dimension-level scores.

The discussion distinguishes structural difficulty from strategic deprioritization (e.g., declining environmental reporting after 2023 vs. persistently absent moderation-labor reporting), which is a more nuanced claim than 'reporting is bad' and is well supported by the within-provider longitudinal figures.
Comprehensive supporting material: stratified sampling procedure, search terms, PRISMA-style flow diagram, per-provider over-time reporting heatmaps, and variance decomposition.
weaknesses: The headline first-party vs. third-party comparison (0.77 vs 2.64) is potentially confounded by document genre: first-party materials are predominantly release-time model/system cards and blogs, while third-party sources are mostly peer-reviewed papers, which are structurally longer and more methodologically detailed. The paper does not adequately disentangle reporting incentives from document-type conventions, despite this being its central 'division of labor' claim.

The scoring rubric measures disclosure specificity, not evaluation quality; a company scoring 3 on sensitive content could be reporting a flawed benchmark. The authors acknowledge this, but the abstract's framing ('third-party evaluators provide broader, more rigorous coverage') slightly overstates what presence-and-detail scores can establish.

Third-party source discovery relies on Paperfinder plus keyword searches filtered to peer-reviewed work, which likely under-samples third-party evaluations (blogs, audits, civil-society reports), and the authors themselves note deduplication problems may inflate evaluation counts. Selection bias toward popular US/China models is acknowledged but only qualitatively corrected for.

The small interview sample (n=10, nearly all US-based, recruited via snowball from authors' contacts) is appropriate for contextualization but the paper's causal claims about organizational incentives rest heavily on it; quote selection by a single author introduces interpretive subjectivity.

Longitudinal 'declining reporting' claims rest on unbalanced quarterly aggregates with as few as 1-4 models per quarter in early years (Fig. 3), and the model's own year-smooth posterior intervals are wide; the descriptive trend is plausible but the statistical support for a sharp post-2023 Q3 drop is thinner than the text implies.

Reproducibility artifacts are incomplete at review time: the code and dataset URLs in App. O and the dataset link on page 2 are placeholders. For a paper whose main contribution is an annotated dataset, this must be resolved before camera-ready.

Category 7 (data/content moderation labor) has zero third-party observations and weakly identified posteriors; the corresponding claims in the abstract about third-party coverage of this dimension should be more carefully hedged.

Fit for ICML is arguable: this is a governance/measurement-audit study rather than a machine learning methods contribution, though it aligns with the growing evaluation-methodology strand at the venue.
